title: Teachers Deserve Better Access to Educational Evidence
author: Science of Learning
summary: The Science of Learning newsletter introduces 'The Evidence Checker,' an AI-assisted tool designed to help teachers navigate the overwhelming and often contradictory world of educational research. The tool generates structured prompts that push AI systems like ChatGPT to give nuanced, evidence-calibrated answers to practical classroom questions rather than vague inspirational language. The authors argue that the traditional intermediary system -- consultants, publishers, PD providers, edu-celebrities -- has left teachers without direct access to research and has allowed ideological, commercial, and institutional pressures to shape the knowledge that reaches classrooms, leading to chronic 'instructional churn.' Generative AI may now democratize that access, letting teachers directly interrogate claims and evaluate evidence quality without specialized expertise. The article provides concrete usage examples and follow-up prompting strategies for deepening the inquiry.
points: * 'The Evidence Checker' generates structured AI prompts from teacher questions, pushing LLMs toward critical, evidence-calibrated responses rather than generic 'best practice' lists. * Educational research has long been filtered through intermediaries whose incentives do not always align with evidence quality -- creating chronic 'instructional churn.' * The power structure has historically privileged those promoting ideas over classroom teachers, who were expected to trust summaries and institutional messaging without examining underlying evidence. * AI may shift this structure by giving teachers direct, interrogative access to the research conversation previously available only to specialists. * The tool is not a replacement for professional judgment but a way to level the epistemic playing field between teachers and those promoting educational ideas.
quotes: Teachers are surrounded by educational claims.
For many classroom teachers, systematically sorting through all of this isn't realistic.

Instead of generating vague inspirational language or simplistic lists of 'best practices,' the AI is instructed to critically evaluate the existing research literature, distinguish between strong and weak evidence, explain important caveats and limitations.

Those promoting educational ideas have had privileged access to research interpretation, while classroom teachers were expected to trust summaries, presentations, institutional messaging, or professional consensus without being able to easily examine the evidence for themselves.
In that sense, this has partly been an issue of power and accountability.
When access to evidence becomes more widely distributed, the professional conversation may begin to shift as well.
Teaching is too important to be driven by slogans, trends, and competing ideologies.
